The linear independence of 11, ζ⁡(3)\zeta(3), and ζ⁡(4)\zeta(4)

Li Lai
Abstract

In a recent breakthrough, Fauzan proved the irrationality of ζ⁡(5)\zeta(5). In this paper, we combine Fauzan’s determinant method with classical simultaneous approximations of zeta values studied by Zudilin and Dauguet–Zudilin to prove the linear independence of 11, ζ⁡(3)\zeta(3), and ζ⁡(4)\zeta(4) over ℚ\mathbb{Q}.

1 Introduction

The special values of the Riemann zeta function

ζ⁡(s)≔∑m=1∞1ms(s=2,3,…)\zeta(s)\coloneq\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{m^{s}}\quad(s=2,3,\ldots)

are natural mathematical constants. They appear frequently in number theory, combinatorics, and theoretical physics. In the eighteenth century, Euler proved that ζ⁡(2​k)/π2​k∈ℚ×\zeta(2k)/\pi^{2k}\in\mathbb{Q}^{\times} for any positive integer kk. In contrast, the arithmetic nature of odd zeta values ζ⁡(2​k+1)\zeta(2k+1) (k∈ℤ>0k\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}) remains mysterious. A folklore conjecture predicts the following.

Conjecture 1.1.

π,ζ⁡(3),ζ⁡(5),…,ζ⁡(2​k+1),…\pi,\zeta(3),\zeta(5),\ldots,\zeta(2k+1),\ldots are algebraically independent over ℚ\mathbb{Q}.

Conjecture 1.1 remains far out of reach; very little is known. Apéry made the first breakthrough:

Theorem 1.2 (Apéry [1], 1979).

The real number ζ⁡(3)\zeta(3) is irrational.

Apéry’s announcement in 1978 came as a surprise. A few months later, Beukers [3] gave an elegant proof of the irrationality of ζ⁡(3)\zeta(3), which is perhaps the most widely known one. Nowadays, many other proofs and explanations of Apéry’s theorem (Theorem 1.2) are available; see [4, 5, 6, 7, 11, 14, 21, 22, 27, 34, 35, 36, 37, 38, 39, 44, 46, 47, 48, 55].

The next breakthrough was made by Ball and Rivoal:

Theorem 1.3 (Rivoal [40], 2000; Ball–Rivoal [2], 2001).

As s→+∞s\to+\infty through odd integers,

dimℚSpanℚ⁡{1,ζ⁡(3),ζ⁡(5),…,ζ⁡(s)}⩾1−o⁡(1)1+log⁡2⋅log⁡s.\dim_{\mathbb{Q}}\operatorname{Span}_{\mathbb{Q}}\{1,\zeta(3),\zeta(5),\ldots,\zeta(s)\}\geqslant\frac{1-o(1)}{1+\log 2}\cdot\log s.

In particular, there are infinitely many irrational odd zeta values.

The dimension lower bound in Theorem 1.3 has been significantly improved to 0.21​s/log⁡s0.21\sqrt{s/\log s} by Fischler [16] for all sufficiently large odd integers ss.

Before the AI age, a remarkable result was achieved by Calegari, Dimitrov, and Tang:

Theorem 1.4 (Calegari–Dimitrov–Tang [8], 2024+).

The three real numbers 11, ζ⁡(2)\zeta(2), and L⁡(2,χ−3)L(2,\chi_{-3}) are linearly independent over ℚ\mathbb{Q}, where L⁡(2,χ−3)=1−2−2−2+4−2−5−2+⋯L(2,\chi_{-3})=1^{-2}-2^{-2}+4^{-2}-5^{-2}+\cdots is a Dirichlet LL-value.

Although there are many partial results towards the irrationality of odd zeta values [10, 15, 17, 18, 19, 28, 29, 31, 32, 41, 42, 45, 49, 51, 52, 53, 54, 56], none of them is ever close to the irrationality of ζ⁡(5)\zeta(5), until the recent breakthrough of Fauzan:

Theorem 1.5 (Fauzan [13], 2026+).

The real number ζ⁡(5)\zeta(5) is irrational.

Before Fauzan’s breakthrough, the closest results to the irrationality of ζ⁡(5)\zeta(5) are “At least one of ζ⁡(5),ζ⁡(7),ζ⁡(9),ζ⁡(11)\zeta(5),\zeta(7),\zeta(9),\zeta(11) is irrational” by Zudilin [51], and “0<|ζ⁡(5)−pn/qn|<qn−0.860<|\zeta(5)-p_{n}/q_{n}|<q_{n}^{-0.86} for an explicit rational sequence pn/qnp_{n}/q_{n}” by Brown–Zudilin [10]. Fauzan’s proof uses Hankel determinants, which were previously studied by Haynes–Zudilin [23] and Zudilin [55]. Fauzan’s proof is also related to some ideas of Brown [9]. Roughly speaking, Hankel determinants yield finer pp-adic estimates.

Fauzan’s determinant method is quite flexible. It quickly led to several further results:

  • •

    Kinali [26] proved the irrationality of the 22-adic zeta value ζ2​(7)\zeta_{2}(7);

  • •

    Liu [33] formalized a proof in Lean 4 of the irrationality of Li2⁡(1/n)\operatorname{Li}_{2}(1/n) for any n∈ℤ∖{0,1}n\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0,1\};

  • •

    Tang [50] formalized a proof in Lean 4 of the linear independence of 11, ζ⁡(2)\zeta(2), and ζ⁡(3)\zeta(3) over ℚ\mathbb{Q}.

The author apologizes for any possible omissions. In the AI age, many recent results have not appeared on arXiv, which makes it difficult to keep track of all of them. In fact, after Fauzan’s breakthrough, Zudilin obtained the irrationality of Li2⁡(1/n)\operatorname{Li}_{2}(1/n) for n∈ℤ∖{0,1}n\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0,1\} before Liu [33]. But Liu was the first to make a Lean 4 proof public. The current author also obtained an AI-generated proof of the linear independence of 11, ζ⁡(2)\zeta(2), and ζ⁡(3)\zeta(3), which is independent of, but a few hours later, than Tang [50]. Therefore, the author gave up to write down a proof for that. Moreover, Zudilin have proved that at least one of L⁡(2,χ−4)L(2,\chi_{-4}) and L⁡(4,χ−4)L(4,\chi_{-4}) is irrational. The irrationality of Catalan’s constant L⁡(2,χ−4)L(2,\chi_{-4}) seems to be a worthwhile goal.

In this paper, we obtain another follow-up result. Our main theorem is the following:

Theorem 1.6.

The three real numbers 11, ζ⁡(3)\zeta(3), and ζ⁡(4)\zeta(4) are linearly independent over ℚ\mathbb{Q}.

The proof just combines Fauzan’s determinant method [13] with Dauguet and Zudilin’s simultaneous approximations of zeta values [11]. After Fauzan’s breakthrough, such quick result is more like an exercise, as commended by Zudilin and agreed by the author. Nevertheness, the author decided to write this paper with the aim of helping himself understand Fauzan’s determinant method. As we shall see, the method is elementary, and the determinant structure strengthens the pp-adic estimates.

Perhaps the most interesting corollary of Theorem 1.6 is the irrationality of ζ⁡(3)/π4\zeta(3)/\pi^{4}. Note that the irrationality of ζ⁡(3)/π2\zeta(3)/\pi^{2} follows from [50]. However, to the best of the author’s knowledge, the irrationality of ζ⁡(3)/π3\zeta(3)/\pi^{3} remains open.

We give an outline of the proof of Theorem 1.6. Suppose that a​ζ​(3)+b​ζ​(4)=ca\zeta(3)+b\zeta(4)=c for integers a,b,ca,b,c, not all being zeros. In Section 2, we associate to this relation a sequence of rational Hankel determinants JnJ_{n}. Their rationality follows from a partial fraction decomposition of the underlying rational function. In Section 3, an auxiliary-prime argument shows that Jn≠0J_{n}\neq 0 for infinitely many nn. In Sections 4 and 5, to estimate the denominators, we group the poles by their residue classes modulo each prime and estimate minors of the resulting local matrices. Their rank restrictions and divisibility give substantially stronger bounds than an entrywise estimate. After summation over the primes, the product formula gives

∑pvp​(Jn)​log⁡p⩾−(30.83+o⁡(1))​n2as ​n→∞.\sum_{p}v_{p}(J_{n})\log p\geqslant-(30.83+o(1))n^{2}\quad\text{as }n\to\infty.

On the other hand, in Section 6, a contour representation, Heine’s identity, and orthogonal polynomials give

|Jn|⩽e−31.6⋅n2\left|J_{n}\right|\leqslant e^{-31.6\cdot n^{2}}

for all sufficiently large nn. These bounds contradict each other along the infinite nonzero subsequence.

By Apéry’s theorem (Theorem 1.2), we must have b≠0b\neq 0. Throughout the paper, until we finally obtain a contradiction, we fix a choice of such integers aa, bb, and cc. For later reference, we record our assumption below:

a​ζ​(3)+b​ζ​(4)=c,a,b,c∈ℤ,b≠0.a\zeta(3)+b\zeta(4)=c,\quad a,b,c\in\mathbb{Z},\quad b\neq 0. (2.1)

3 Nonvanishing of the determinants

In this section, we prove that Jn≠0J_{n}\neq 0 infinitely often. The method is by using auxiliary primes qq. This idea appeared before in the study of pp-adic zeta values by Sprang and the author [30].

Proposition 3.1.

Let qq be a prime number such that q≡1(mod9)q\equiv 1\pmod{9} and q>|b|q>|b|. Set m=(q−1)/9m=(q-1)/9, then J2​m≠0J_{2m}\neq 0. In particular, there are infinitely many positive integers nn such that Jn≠0J_{n}\neq 0.

4 pp-adic estimates for the determinants

As we have shown, under the assumption (2.1), we have Jn∈ℚJ_{n}\in\mathbb{Q}. In this section, we will give a lower bound for the pp-adic order of JnJ_{n} prime-by-prime. For any prime pp, denote by logp\log_{p} the logarithm with respect to the base pp. As usual, vp​(x)v_{p}(x) denotes the pp-adic order for any x∈ℚx\in\mathbb{Q}, normalized by vp​(p)=1v_{p}(p)=1 with the convention vp​(0)=+∞v_{p}(0)=+\infty. We first recall the classical pp-adic estimates.

Lemma 4.1 (classical pp-adic estimates).

The following pp-adic estimates hold.

  1. (1)

    For any prime pp,

    vp​(Jn)⩾−12​n​logp⁡(8​n).v_{p}(J_{n})\geqslant-12n\log_{p}(8n).
  2. (2)

    For any prime p>8​np>\sqrt{8n},

    vp​(Jn)⩾−12​n.v_{p}(J_{n})\geqslant-12n.
  3. (3)

    For any prime p>6​np>6n,

    vp​(Jn)⩾0.v_{p}(J_{n})\geqslant 0.
Proof.

Consider the new basis (t0)\binom{t}{0}, (t1)\binom{t}{1}, (t2)\binom{t}{2}, …\ldots, (t3​n−1)\binom{t}{3n-1} of the space ℚ​[t]<3​n\mathbb{Q}[t]_{<3n}. The transfer matrix form the old basis 1,t,t2,…,t3​n−11,t,t^{2},\ldots,t^{3n-1} to the new basis is triangular with diagonal entries 1/i!1/i! (i=0,1,…,3​n−1i=0,1,\ldots,3n-1). Therefore, by (2.4) and (2.5),

Jn=det(ℬn​((ti),(tj)))0⩽i,j<3​n=det(ℒn​((ti)⋅(tj)))0⩽i,j<3​n.J_{n}=\det\left(\mathcal{B}_{n}\left(\binom{t}{i},\binom{t}{j}\right)\right)_{0\leqslant i,j<3n}=\det\left(\mathcal{L}_{n}\left(\binom{t}{i}\cdot\binom{t}{j}\right)\right)_{0\leqslant i,j<3n}. (4.1)

It is elementary (see Zudilin [54, Lemma 15]) to show that

lcm⁡[1,2,…,i]⋅dd​t​(ti)|t=−k∈ℤfor any k∈ℤ and i∈ℤ>0.\operatorname{lcm}[1,2,\ldots,i]\cdot\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\binom{t}{i}\Big|_{t=-k}\in\mathbb{Z}\quad\text{for any $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $i\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}$}.

Therefore,

vp​(dd​t​(ti)|t=−k)⩾−⌊logp⁡(3​n)⌋for any k∈ℤ and i∈{0,1,…,3​n−1}.v_{p}\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\binom{t}{i}\Big|_{t=-k}\right)\geqslant-\lfloor\log_{p}(3n)\rfloor\quad\text{for any $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $i\in\{0,1,\ldots,3n-1\}$}. (4.2)

By (2.6), for any 0⩽i,j<3​n0\leqslant i,j<3n we have

ℒn​((ti)⋅(tj))\displaystyle\ \mathcal{L}_{n}\left(\binom{t}{i}\cdot\binom{t}{j}\right)
=\displaystyle= ∑k=06​n(6​nk)2​(2​n+kk)3​(Uk​(−ki)​dd​t​(tj)|t=−k+Uk​(−kj)​dd​t​(ti)|t=−k+Vk​(−ki)​(−kj)),\displaystyle\ \sum_{k=0}^{6n}\binom{6n}{k}^{2}\binom{2n+k}{k}^{3}\left(U_{k}\binom{-k}{i}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\binom{t}{j}\Big|_{t=-k}+U_{k}\binom{-k}{j}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\binom{t}{i}\Big|_{t=-k}+V_{k}\binom{-k}{i}\binom{-k}{j}\right), (4.3)

where UkU_{k} and VkV_{k} are given by (2.7) and (2.8).

Now, for any prime pp, since vp​(Hk(s))⩾−s⁡⌊logp⁡k⌋v_{p}(H_{k}^{(s)})\geqslant-s\lfloor\log_{p}k\rfloor for any k,s∈ℤ>0k,s\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}, we have

vp​(Uk)⩾−3​⌊logp⁡(6​n)⌋,vp​(Vk)⩾−4​⌊logp⁡(8​n)⌋,k∈{0,1,…,6​n}.v_{p}\left(U_{k}\right)\geqslant-3\lfloor\log_{p}(6n)\rfloor,\quad v_{p}\left(V_{k}\right)\geqslant-4\lfloor\log_{p}(8n)\rfloor,\quad k\in\{0,1,\ldots,6n\}. (4.4)

Combining (4.2)–(4.4),

vp​(ℒn​((ti)⋅(tj)))⩾−4​⌊logp⁡(8​n)⌋for any prime p and ​i,j∈{0,1,…,3​n−1}.v_{p}\left(\mathcal{L}_{n}\left(\binom{t}{i}\cdot\binom{t}{j}\right)\right)\geqslant-4\lfloor\log_{p}(8n)\rfloor\quad\text{for any prime $p$ and }i,j\in\{0,1,\ldots,3n-1\}. (4.5)

By (4.1) and (4.5), we obtain

vp​(Jn)⩾−12​n​⌊logp⁡(8​n)⌋,v_{p}(J_{n})\geqslant-12n\lfloor\log_{p}(8n)\rfloor,

which proves both (1) and (2).

Finally, for (3), note that for any p>6​np>6n and k∈{0,1,…,6​n}k\in\{0,1,\ldots,6n\}, we have

vp​((2​n+kk)​H2​n+k)⩾0⟹vp​((2​n+kk)​Vk)⩾0.v_{p}\left(\binom{2n+k}{k}H_{2n+k}\right)\geqslant 0\Longrightarrow v_{p}\left(\binom{2n+k}{k}V_{k}\right)\geqslant 0.

Clearly, vp​(Uk)⩾0v_{p}(U_{k})\geqslant 0 and vp​(dd​t​(ti)|t=−k)⩾0v_{p}\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\binom{t}{i}\big|_{t=-k}\right)\geqslant 0 by (4.2). Therefore, (4.3) implies

vp​(ℒn​((ti)⋅(tj)))⩾0for any prime p>6​n and ​i,j∈{0,1,…,3​n−1}.v_{p}\left(\mathcal{L}_{n}\left(\binom{t}{i}\cdot\binom{t}{j}\right)\right)\geqslant 0\quad\text{for any prime $p>6n$ and }i,j\in\{0,1,\ldots,3n-1\}.

Thus, (4.1) implies vp​(Jn)⩾0v_{p}(J_{n})\geqslant 0 for any prime p>6​np>6n, proving (3). ∎

In the rest of this section, we will establish finer pp-adic estimates for primes 8​n<p⩽6​n\sqrt{8n}<p\leqslant 6n. This is the key advantage of Fauzan’s determinant method. In spirit, these finer pp-adic estimates can be viewed as a kind of generalization of the Φn\Phi_{n}-factor method of Zudilin [51, 54].

+3⋅max{0,m−2⌊6​n−ρp⌋}+𝟏m=1⋅𝟏p>max⁡{6​n−ρ,2​n+ρ}.\displaystyle\ +3\cdot\max\left\{0,m-2\left\lfloor\frac{6n-\rho}{p}\right\rfloor\right\}+\mathbf{1}_{m=1}\cdot\mathbf{1}_{p>\max\{6n-\rho,2n+\rho\}}. (4.8)

For any prime 8​n<p⩽6​n\sqrt{8n}<p\leqslant 6n and ρ∈{0,1,…,p−1}\rho\in\{0,1,\ldots,p-1\}, for any subsets I,J⊂{0,1,…,3​n−1}I,J\subset\{0,1,\ldots,3n-1\} of size |I|=|J|=m∈ℤ⩾0|I|=|J|=m\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geqslant 0}, we have

In this section, we estimate |Jn||J_{n}| as a real number. Recall the linear operator ℒn\mathcal{L}_{n} is defined by (2.3). We first express it as a contour integral. This is a classical argument, Nesterenko [34], Rivoal [41], and Zudilin [51, 52, 53, 54] have studied such integrals extensively.

By symmetry and continuity, we may fix a y>0y>0. By (2.2), we have

log⁡|Rn​(2​n+12+𝐢​n​y)|\displaystyle\ \log\left|R_{n}\left(2n+\frac{1}{2}+\mathbf{i}ny\right)\right|
=\displaystyle= log⁡(6n)!2(2n)!3+32​∑k=12​nlog⁡(n2​y2+(k−12)2)−∑j=06​nlog⁡(n2​y2+(2​n+j+12)2)\displaystyle\ \log\frac{(6n)!^{2}}{(2n)!^{3}}+\frac{3}{2}\sum_{k=1}^{2n}\log\left(n^{2}y^{2}+\left(k-\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}\right)-\sum_{j=0}^{6n}\log\left(n^{2}y^{2}+\left(2n+j+\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}\right)
=\displaystyle= log⁡(6n)!2n6​n+2(2n)!3+32​∑k=12​ng⁡(k−12n)−∑j=06​ng⁡(2+j+12n)\displaystyle\ \log\frac{(6n)!^{2}}{n^{6n+2}(2n)!^{3}}+\frac{3}{2}\sum_{k=1}^{2n}g\left(\frac{k-\frac{1}{2}}{n}\right)-\sum_{j=0}^{6n}g\left(2+\frac{j+\frac{1}{2}}{n}\right) (6.4)

where the function gg is given by

g⁡(x)≔log⁡(x2+y2),x∈ℝ.g(x)\coloneq\log(x^{2}+y^{2}),\quad x\in\mathbb{R}.

It is natural to compare the sum of values of gg with its integral. Note that

x​log⁡(x2+y2)−2​x+2​y​arctan⁡xyx\log(x^{2}+y^{2})-2x+2y\arctan\frac{x}{y}

is a primitive function of g⁡(x)g(x). Since gg is increasing on (0,+∞)(0,+\infty), we obtain

∑k=12​ng⁡(k−12n)\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{2n}g\left(\frac{k-\frac{1}{2}}{n}\right) ⩽12​g​(2−12​n)+n​∫12​n2g⁡(x)​𝑑x⩽12​g​(2)+n​∫12​n2g⁡(x)​𝑑x\displaystyle\leqslant\frac{1}{2}g\left(2-\frac{1}{2n}\right)+n\int_{\frac{1}{2n}}^{2}g(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\leqslant\frac{1}{2}g(2)+n\int_{\frac{1}{2n}}^{2}g(x)\,\mathrm{d}x
=(2​log⁡(y2+4)−4+2​y​arctan​2y)​n+12​log​y2+4y2+14​n2+1−2​n​y​arctan​12​n​y\displaystyle=\left(2\log(y^{2}+4)-4+2y\arctan\frac{2}{y}\right)n+\frac{1}{2}\log\frac{y^{2}+4}{y^{2}+\frac{1}{4n^{2}}}+1-2ny\arctan\frac{1}{2ny}
⩽(2​log⁡(y2+4)−4+2​y​arctan⁡2y)​n+log⁡(4​n)+1,\displaystyle\leqslant\left(2\log(y^{2}+4)-4+2y\arctan\frac{2}{y}\right)n+\log(4n)+1, (6.5)

and

∑j=06​ng⁡(2+j+12n)\displaystyle\sum_{j=0}^{6n}g\left(2+\frac{j+\frac{1}{2}}{n}\right) ⩾12​g​(2+12​n)+12​g​(8+12​n)+n​∫28g⁡(x)​𝑑x\displaystyle\geqslant\frac{1}{2}g\left(2+\frac{1}{2n}\right)+\frac{1}{2}g\left(8+\frac{1}{2n}\right)+n\int_{2}^{8}g(x)\,\mathrm{d}x
>(8​log⁡(y2+64)−2​log⁡(y2+4)+2​y​arctan​8y−2​y​arctan​2y−12)​n\displaystyle>\left(8\log(y^{2}+64)-2\log(y^{2}+4)+2y\arctan\frac{8}{y}-2y\arctan\frac{2}{y}-12\right)n
+log⁡2+log⁡8\displaystyle\quad+\log 2+\log 8 (6.6)

Substituting (6.5) and (6.6) into (6.4), and using the well-known inequality

2​π​m​(me)m⩽m!⩽2​π​m​(me)m​e112​m,m∈ℤ>0,\sqrt{2\pi m}\left(\frac{m}{e}\right)^{m}\leqslant m!\leqslant\sqrt{2\pi m}\left(\frac{m}{e}\right)^{m}e^{\frac{1}{12m}},\quad m\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0},

we easily complete the proof. ∎

Lemma 6.3.

For any z=2​n+1/2+𝐢​xz=2n+1/2+\mathbf{i}x with x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}, we have

|12​π​Rn​(z)​(πsin⁡π​z)2​(3​a−2​b​π​cot⁡(π​z))|⩽103​(|a|+|b|)​n−1⋅ec1​n​e−c2​|x|,\left|\frac{1}{2\pi}R_{n}(z)\left(\frac{\pi}{\sin\pi z}\right)^{2}\Big(3a-2b\pi\cot(\pi z)\Big)\right|\leqslant 10^{3}\left(|a|+|b|\right)n^{-1}\cdot e^{c_{1}n}e^{-c_{2}|x|},

where

c1=G⁡(45)−45​G′​(45)<0,c2=2​π−G′​(45)>0.c_{1}=G\left(\frac{4}{5}\right)-\frac{4}{5}G^{\prime}\left(\frac{4}{5}\right)<0,\qquad c_{2}=2\pi-G^{\prime}\left(\frac{4}{5}\right)>0. (6.7)

The function G⁡(y)G(y) is given by (6.3).

Proof.

We have

|πsin⁡π​z|\displaystyle\left|\frac{\pi}{\sin\pi z}\right| =2​πeπ​x+e−π​x⩽2​π​e−π​|x|,\displaystyle=\frac{2\pi}{e^{\pi x}+e^{-\pi x}}\leqslant 2\pi e^{-\pi|x|},
|cot⁡π​z|\displaystyle\left|\cot\pi z\right| =|eπ​x−e−π​xeπ​x+e−π​x|⩽1.\displaystyle=\left|\frac{e^{\pi x}-e^{-\pi x}}{e^{\pi x}+e^{-\pi x}}\right|\leqslant 1.

By Lemma 6.2 with y=x/ny=x/n, we have

|Rn​(z)|⩽10n​en​G​(x/n)=10n​en​G​(|x|/n),|R_{n}(z)|\leqslant\frac{10}{n}e^{nG(x/n)}=\frac{10}{n}e^{nG(|x|/n)},

where the function GG is given by (6.3). Putting the above estimates together, we obtain

|12​π​Rn​(z)​(πsin⁡π​z)2​(3​a−2​b​π​cot⁡(π​z))|⩽103​(|a|+|b|)​n−1⋅exp⁡(−2​π​|x|+n​G​(|x|n)).\left|\frac{1}{2\pi}R_{n}(z)\left(\frac{\pi}{\sin\pi z}\right)^{2}\Big(3a-2b\pi\cot(\pi z)\Big)\right|\leqslant 10^{3}\left(|a|+|b|\right)n^{-1}\cdot\exp\left(-2\pi|x|+nG\left(\frac{|x|}{n}\right)\right). (6.8)

Now, a direct calculation on (6.3) gives

G′​(y)=5​arctan⁡2y−2​arctan⁡8y,G′′​(y)=6​(y2−96)(y2+4)​(y2+64).G^{\prime}(y)=5\arctan\frac{2}{y}-2\arctan\frac{8}{y},\quad G^{\prime\prime}(y)=\frac{6(y^{2}-96)}{(y^{2}+4)(y^{2}+64)}.

Let

λ0=G′​(45)=5​arctan⁡52−2​arctan⁡10=3.009194​….\lambda_{0}=G^{\prime}\left(\frac{4}{5}\right)=5\arctan\frac{5}{2}-2\arctan 10=3.009194\ldots.

The function G′​(y)−λ0G^{\prime}(y)-\lambda_{0} is decreasing on (0,96](0,\sqrt{96}] and increasing on [96,+∞)[\sqrt{96},+\infty) with limy→+∞(G′​(y)−λ0)=−λ0<0\lim_{y\to+\infty}(G^{\prime}(y)-\lambda_{0})=-\lambda_{0}<0. Therefore, G′​(y)−λ0G^{\prime}(y)-\lambda_{0} is positive on (0,4/5)(0,4/5) and negative on (4/5,+∞)(4/5,+\infty). So

G(y)−λ0y⩽G(45)−45λ0=c1,for all y∈[0,+∞).G(y)-\lambda_{0}y\leqslant G\left(\frac{4}{5}\right)-\frac{4}{5}\lambda_{0}=c_{1},\quad\text{for all }y\in[0,+\infty).

Thus,

n​G​(|x|n)⩽c1​n+λ0​|x|.nG\left(\frac{|x|}{n}\right)\leqslant c_{1}n+\lambda_{0}|x|.

Substituting this into (6.8) comletes the proof. ∎

Lemma 6.4.

For any integer n⩾2⋅103​(|a|+|b|)n\geqslant 2\cdot 10^{3}(|a|+|b|), we have

|Jn|⩽e3​c1​n223​n(3n)!∏k=03​n−1k!2​∫ℝ3​n∏1⩽i<j⩽3​n(xi−xj)2​∏ℓ=13​ne−c2​|xℓ|​d​xℓ,|J_{n}|\leqslant\frac{e^{3c_{1}n^{2}}}{2^{3n}(3n)!\prod_{k=0}^{3n-1}k!^{2}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3n}}\prod_{1\leqslant i<j\leqslant 3n}(x_{i}-x_{j})^{2}\prod_{\ell=1}^{3n}e^{-c_{2}|x_{\ell}|}\,\mathrm{d}x_{\ell},

where c1,c2c_{1},c_{2} are given by (6.7).

Proof.

By (2.5) and Lemma 6.1, we have

Jn=1∏k=03​n−1k!2​det(∫−∞+∞(2​n+12+𝐢​x)i+j​ω​(x)​𝑑x)0⩽i,j<3​n,J_{n}=\frac{1}{\prod_{k=0}^{3n-1}k!^{2}}\det\left(\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\left(2n+\frac{1}{2}+\mathbf{i}x\right)^{i+j}\omega(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\right)_{0\leqslant i,j<3n},

where

ω⁡(x)=12​π​Rn​(z)​(πsin⁡π​z)2​(3​a−2​b​π​cot⁡(π​z))|z=2​n+1/2+𝐢​x.\omega(x)=\frac{1}{2\pi}R_{n}(z)\left(\frac{\pi}{\sin\pi z}\right)^{2}\Big(3a-2b\pi\cot(\pi z)\Big)\Big|_{z=2n+1/2+\mathbf{i}x}.

By Heine’s identity [25] (which is a nice application of Fubini’s theorem, see also Zudilin [55, p. 304]), we obtain

Jn=1∏k=03​n−1k!2⋅𝐢3​n​(3​n−1)(3​n)!∫ℝ3​n∏1⩽i<j⩽3​n(xi−xj)2∏ℓ=13​nω(xℓ)dxℓ.J_{n}=\frac{1}{\prod_{k=0}^{3n-1}k!^{2}}\cdot\frac{\mathbf{i}^{3n(3n-1)}}{(3n)!}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3n}}\prod_{1\leqslant i<j\leqslant 3n}(x_{i}-x_{j})^{2}\prod_{\ell=1}^{3n}\omega(x_{\ell})\,\mathrm{d}x_{\ell}.

By Lemma 6.3,

|Jn|⩽(103​(|a|+|b|)n)3​n⋅e3​c1​n2(3n)!∏k=03​n−1k!2∫ℝ3​n∏1⩽i<j⩽3​n(xi−xj)2∏ℓ=13​ne−c2​|xℓ|dxℓ.|J_{n}|\leqslant\left(\frac{10^{3}(|a|+|b|)}{n}\right)^{3n}\cdot\frac{e^{3c_{1}n^{2}}}{(3n)!\prod_{k=0}^{3n-1}k!^{2}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3n}}\prod_{1\leqslant i<j\leqslant 3n}(x_{i}-x_{j})^{2}\prod_{\ell=1}^{3n}e^{-c_{2}|x_{\ell}|}\,\mathrm{d}x_{\ell}.

This completes the proof. ∎

We need one last lemma, which is an evaluation of multiple integral.

Lemma 6.5.

We have

123​n(3n)!∏k=03​n−1k!2​∫ℝ3​n∏1⩽i<j⩽3​n(xi−xj)2​∏ℓ=13​n2ec2​xℓ+e−c2​xℓ​d​xℓ=(π2​c2)9​n2.\frac{1}{2^{3n}(3n)!\prod_{k=0}^{3n-1}k!^{2}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3n}}\prod_{1\leqslant i<j\leqslant 3n}(x_{i}-x_{j})^{2}\prod_{\ell=1}^{3n}\frac{2}{e^{c_{2}x_{\ell}}+e^{-c_{2}x_{\ell}}}\,\mathrm{d}x_{\ell}=\left(\frac{\pi}{2c_{2}}\right)^{9n^{2}}.
Proof.

Apply the change of variables xℓ=(π/c2)​yℓx_{\ell}=(\pi/c_{2})y_{\ell}, ℓ=1,2,…,3​n\ell=1,2,\ldots,3n. The assertion of this lemma is equivalent to

1(3​n)!​∫ℝ3​n∏1⩽i<j⩽3​n(yi−yj)2​∏ℓ=13​n2eπ​yℓ+e−π​yℓ​d​yℓ=∏k=03​n−1k!24k.\frac{1}{(3n)!}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3n}}\prod_{1\leqslant i<j\leqslant 3n}(y_{i}-y_{j})^{2}\prod_{\ell=1}^{3n}\frac{2}{e^{\pi y_{\ell}}+e^{-\pi y_{\ell}}}\,\mathrm{d}y_{\ell}=\prod_{k=0}^{3n-1}\frac{k!^{2}}{4^{k}}. (6.9)

For the weight function ω⁡(y)=2/(eπ​y+e−π​y)\omega(y)=2/(e^{\pi y}+e^{-\pi y}) on ℝ\mathbb{R}, the corresponding orthogonal polynomials are known [12, 24]. By [24, Equations (5.9.8) and (5.9.9)], there exist polynomials Pk​(y)∈ℚ​[y]P_{k}(y)\in\mathbb{Q}[y] (k∈ℤ⩾0k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geqslant 0}) with deg⁡Pk=k\deg P_{k}=k and leading coefficients [yk]​(Pk)=2k/k![y^{k}](P_{k})=2^{k}/k! such that

∫ℝPj​(y)​Pk​(y)​2eπ​y+e−π​y​𝑑y=δj,k,j,k∈ℤ⩾0.\int_{\mathbb{R}}P_{j}(y)P_{k}(y)\frac{2}{e^{\pi y}+e^{-\pi y}}\,\mathrm{d}y=\delta_{j,k},\quad j,k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geqslant 0}.

Then, using Heine’s identity again,

1(3​n)!​∫ℝ3​n(det(Pk​(yj+1))0⩽j,k<3​n)2​∏ℓ=13​n2eπ​yℓ+e−π​yℓ​d​yℓ=1.\frac{1}{(3n)!}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3n}}\left(\det\Big(P_{k}(y_{j+1})\Big)_{0\leqslant j,k<3n}\right)^{2}\prod_{\ell=1}^{3n}\frac{2}{e^{\pi y_{\ell}}+e^{-\pi y_{\ell}}}\,\mathrm{d}y_{\ell}=1.

Since the transfer matrix from 1,y,y2,…,y3​n−11,y,y^{2},\ldots,y^{3n-1} to P0​(y),P1​(y),…,P3​n−1​(y)P_{0}(y),P_{1}(y),\ldots,P_{3n-1}(y) is triangular with diagonal entries 2k/k!2^{k}/k! (k=0,1,…,3​n−1k=0,1,\ldots,3n-1), we have

det(Pk​(yj+1))0⩽j,k<3​n=∏k=03​n−12kk!⋅∏1⩽i<j⩽3​n(yj−yi),\det\Big(P_{k}(y_{j+1})\Big)_{0\leqslant j,k<3n}=\prod_{k=0}^{3n-1}\frac{2^{k}}{k!}\cdot\prod_{1\leqslant i<j\leqslant 3n}(y_{j}-y_{i}),

which proves (6.9). ∎

Proposition 6.6.

For any integer n⩾2⋅103​(|a|+|b|)n\geqslant 2\cdot 10^{3}(|a|+|b|), we have

|Jn|⩽e−31⋅n2.|J_{n}|\leqslant e^{-31\cdot n^{2}}.
Proof.

Since c2>0c_{2}>0 (see (6.7)), we have

e−c2​|x|⩽2ec2​x+e−c2​x,x∈ℝ.e^{-c_{2}|x|}\leqslant\frac{2}{e^{c_{2}x}+e^{-c_{2}x}},\quad x\in\mathbb{R}.

Substituting this into Lemma 6.4 and then using Lemma 6.5, we obtain

|Jn|⩽e−c3​n2,for any ​n⩾2⋅103​(|a|+|b|),|J_{n}|\leqslant e^{-c_{3}n^{2}},\quad\text{for any }n\geqslant 2\cdot 10^{3}(|a|+|b|),

where

c3=9​log⁡2​c2π−3​c1,c_{3}=9\log\frac{2c_{2}}{\pi}-3c_{1},

and c1,c2c_{1},c_{2} are given by (6.7). This c3c_{3} is an explicit constant:

c3\displaystyle c_{3} =9​log⁡(1+10​arctan⁡(2/5)−4​arctan⁡(1/10)π)−3​(12​log​3−32​log​2+5​log​2925−8​log​101100)\displaystyle=9\log\left(1+\frac{10\arctan(2/5)-4\arctan(1/10)}{\pi}\right)-3\left(12\log 3-32\log 2+5\log\frac{29}{25}-8\log\frac{101}{100}\right)
=31.614437​….\displaystyle=31.614437\ldots.

∎

Now, Propositions 3.1, 5.5, and 6.6 give a contradiction. So the assumption (2.1) cannot hold. This proves Theorem 1.6. We conclude this paper by a remark.

Remark 6.7.

One can show a better real estimate by shifting the contour and using the equilibrium measure (see [43]). For the pp-adic estimate in Proposition 5.5, by using more economical estimates in the summation over pp process and a more tedious case-by-case discussion, one can deduce from Lemma 4.4 a better arithmetic estimate. Therefore, the margin in the main theorem is slightly larger than what we proved. Our approach is mainly intended to keep the proof as simple as possible.
